title: Empirical Integration of a Formal Network Verifier as an Oracle inside an LLM Generate–Verify–Repair Loop: A Preregistered Paired Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired within‑task experiment (study_id netverify_gvr_empirical_integration_2026_v1) to measure whether embedding a deterministic network verifier as an oracle inside a bounded LLM Generate–Verify–Repair (GVR) loop increases detection/rejection of unsafe or incorrect LLM‑generated network configurations and improves bounded repair success versus single‑shot generation. Using a synthetic intent→configuration suite (N=270 tasks), gpt-5-mini as the generator, and a Dockerized Kathará/Mininet deterministic validator/emulator as ground truth, the single generated candidate per paired task (shared_initial_candidate semantics) was verifier‑acceptable for every task. Baseline accepted 270/270 (100%); guarded (verify→optional bounded repair) accepted 270/270 (100%); no repairs were invoked. Paired difference = 0.00 (paired bootstrap 95% CI [0.00,0.00], exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; bootstrap resamples = 10,000, seed = 1729). We release the complete preregistration, execution, validator traces, scoring JSONs, and per‑artifact SHA‑256 manifest to enable deterministic reproduction and to show that generation‑semantics (shared candidate vs independent per‑arm sampling) is decisive for whether a verifier insertion can change observed outcomes. We document the minimal, artifact‑grounded recipe required to test the original marginal estimand (make independent_condition_generation=true and enable independent generation per arm).

sections.introduction: Motivation. Large language models (LLMs) can convert operator intent into low‑level device commands but produce stochastic outputs that may be syntactically plausible yet semantically unsafe for networks. Generate–Verify–Repair (GVR) architectures interpose deterministic oracles (verifiers) between stochastic generation and deployment to reduce deployment risk by rejecting unsafe candidates and guiding repair loops with actionable diagnostics. Research question. Does embedding a deterministic network verifier as an oracle inside a bounded LLM GVR loop increase the fraction of unsafe/incorrect LLM‑generated configurations that are detected/rejected and, conditional on rejection, increase bounded repair success relative to single‑shot generation? Contributions. (1) A fully preregistered confirmatory paired experiment (study_id netverify_gvr_empirical_integration_2026_v1) with complete provenance and per‑artifact SHA‑256s. (2) A deterministic, Dockerized execution bundle (Kathará/Mininet emulator + deterministic_netops_validator_v5) and publicized scoring traces for every episode. (3) An empirical outcome that makes explicit how generation semantics (shared_initial_candidate vs independent sampling) deterministically control whether a verifier can change accept/reject counts and therefore whether the original estimand is testable under the executed configuration.
sections.related_work: Context and gap. Generative verification patterns and GVR architectures have been proposed to reduce LLM hallucination and enforce formal correctness in compliance‑sensitive domains (e.g., Cadenas, "Convergent Correctness", doi:10.2139/ssrn.6754899). Domain‑specific deterministic verifiers and quantitative verification frameworks exist for network properties (e.g., weighted NetKAT; Suárez Acevedo et al., doi:10.1145/3808318). Recent NetOps proposals combine intent life‑cycle, RAG, and verifier anchoring (OpenAlex entries W4414359351, W4400072049, W4386722061). Prior work typically supplies architectural arguments or case studies; what is missing is a preregistered, provenance‑anchored paired test that records every generation and verification trace and that makes explicit how sampling semantics affect detectability of verifier benefits. Our study fills that methodological gap by releasing verifiable artifacts that demonstrate a boundary case where a verifier insertion, as executed, produces no measured marginal effect.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and frozen plan. We preregistered the study under netverify_gvr_empirical_integration_2026_v1 before execution (preregistration SHA‑256 8ae7fbadf89e5d56671560e43f03c4a92ad5f8c9b8586ac8eb3cc3c8fa00a1c0). Primary estimand: paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline (within‑task difference in proportion of verifier rejections/accepts). Design. Paired within‑task (Npairs=270) constructed as 3 vendor syntaxes × 3 topology templates × 30 tasks = 270 tasks. A 20% stratified validation subset (54 tasks) was reserved for verifier↔emulator concordance checks. Generator and verifier. Declared generator: gpt-5-mini (execution/model_configuration.json SHA‑256 a40e96e212ab87da251ac0d6dbb75bc543afa13438b5a6b9ebd073597ffdd820; provider recorded as openai_responses). Deterministic verifier: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 executed against a Dockerized Kathará/Mininet emulator used as definitive ground truth. Execution contract and decisive sampling semantics. The preregistered execution_contract set initial_generation_calls_per_task=1 and independent_condition_generation=false (shared_initial_candidate semantics) so a single generated candidate per task was evaluated in both arms; maximum_repair_calls_per_task=1. These exact fields and values are archived in execution/execution_manifest.json (artifact manifest recorded). Scoring. Every candidate was deterministically validated and scored; scoring JSONs include validator_trace (normalized_configuration, parsed_command_count, violation codes, and final validity decision). Example scoring files are in execution/scoring/; representative SHA‑256s are in the artifact manifest. Statistical analysis. Primary test: exact McNemar two‑sided test on paired binary outcomes; paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI with 10,000 resamples (bootstrap_seed=1729) reported. Missingness and retry rules. Model/API call failures: deterministic retry policy (≤2 retries per failed call); retries and infrastructure failures are logged. Repair policy. Guarded arm: if verifier rejects, run a bounded repair loop guided by verifier diagnostics (preregistered maximum_repair_calls_per_task=1). All generation and repair traces were archived.

Discordant pairs: n10=0 (guarded only), n01=0 (baseline only); contingency: n11=270, n10=0, n01=0, n00=0 (see analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv). For the 54‑task validation subset, verifier↔emulator agreement was 54/54 (false_accept=0, false_reject=0) per scoring JSON traces. Statistical inference. Observed paired difference = 0.00. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Paired bootstrap 95% percentile CI = [0.00,0.00] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). Interpretation of these quantities is discussed below.
sections.discussion: Why the run produced a provenance‑backed null. Two preregistered operational choices produced the degenerate contingency: (1) the execution used shared_initial_candidate semantics (execution_contract.independent_condition_generation=false) so a single generated candidate per task was evaluated in both arms; and (2) the chosen generator configuration (gpt-5-mini under the recorded model_configuration.json) produced verifier‑acceptable outputs for every task. Both facts are archived (execution/execution_manifest.json and execution/raw_results.jsonl). Consequence for estimand and power. The preregistered power/MDE calculation assumed independent stochastic generation per arm. Under shared candidate execution the variance used in that calculation is extinguished, invalidating the original MDE/power interpretation for the observed contingency. Numerically, zero discordant pairs (n10=n01=0) force a paired bootstrap CI=[0.00,0.00] and McNemar p=1.0; these numbers are arithmetic consequences of the observed contingency and do not imply the verifier is ‘‘useless’’ in other sampling regimes. Operational lesson. Generation semantics are a primary control parameter: when a single candidate is shared across both arms and the generator produces verifier‑acceptable outputs, inserting a verifier and bounded repair loop cannot change accept/reject counts. This demonstrates a reproducible boundary condition and emphasizes that empirical claims about verifier utility must specify generation sampling semantics. Reproducible minimal follow‑up recipe (artifact‑anchored). The archived harness can deterministically re‑test the original marginal estimand with the minimal changes below (exact JSON fields and artifact paths are present in the preregistration and execution manifest): (A) set execution_contract.independent_condition_generation=true so each arm receives an independent stochastic generation; (B) set maximum_model_calls (or planned_model_calls) ≥ 540 to permit one independent generation per arm per task; (C) modify execution/model_configuration.json to expose sampling (e.g., set a nonzero temperature or supply a seeds list per task) so generator outputs vary across arms; (D) optionally set maximum_repair_calls_per_task>1 to evaluate bounded multi‑attempt repair convergence. All referenced JSON fields and artifact locations appear in the archived preregistration and execution manifest (see execution/*). Threats to validity. Internal validity: the shared candidate choice removed between‑arm stochasticity and changed the effective estimand. Construct validity: the synthetic task bank encodes operationally meaningful patterns (shutdown→change→restore, make‑before‑break) but does not capture full production heterogeneity. External validity: single model (gpt-5-mini) and single verifier rule set were used. Conclusion validity: zero discordant pairs preclude informative rejection of the null in the preregistered sense; this is an artifact‑grounded observation, not evidence that verifiers lack value in broader regimes.
sections.conclusion: We preregistered and executed a fully instrumented paired study integrating a deterministic network verifier into an LLM GVR pipeline and released the full provenance bundle. Under the executed shared_initial_candidate semantics the single generated candidate per task (N=270) was verifier‑acceptable for every task; baseline and guarded final acceptance rates were both 100%, n11=270, n10=0, n01=0, n00=0, paired difference 0.00 (95% bootstrap CI [0.00,0.00]; McNemar p=1.0). The principal scientific contribution is methodological and operational: we show, with artifact‑anchored evidence and immutable hashes, that generation semantics (shared candidate vs independent per‑arm sampling) deterministically control whether a verifier insertion can change observed accept/reject outcomes. We publish an explicit, minimal, artifact‑grounded recipe (set execution_contract.independent_condition_generation=true; increase model call budget; enable sampling) so others can deterministically explore the regime where verifier/repair utility will be observed. All raw model responses, scoring JSONs, validator traces, execution logs, result schema, and per‑artifact SHA‑256 hashes are archived under execution/* and analysis/* to permit deterministic reproduction and targeted follow‑ups (representative manifests and hashes appear in the Disclosure Statement and Table 2).

Reproducibility guidance (artifact‑anchored minimal follow‑up recipe): to test the original marginal estimand with this harness change only the following archived fields and re‑run the harness: set execution_contract.independent_condition_generation=true; increase model call budget (maximum_model_calls ≥ 540) so each arm receives an independent generation; set execution/model_configuration.json sampling parameters (nonzero temperature or per‑task seeds) to enable generator variance; optionally increase maximum_repair_calls_per_task >1 to study bounded repair convergence. All referenced JSON fields and paths exist in the archived preregistration and execution manifest. No human manual manuscript editing occurred after the autonomy lock; all steps and final artifacts contain cryptographic hashes for deterministic verification.
limitations: Synthetic task suite and emulator: tasks are synthetic and validated in a Dockerized Kathará/Mininet emulator; results may not generalize to heterogeneous production devices or live operational conditions.
Single generator: a single declared generator (gpt-5-mini) was used; no claim of multi‑model generality is implied.

Sampling semantics vs preregistered MDE: the preregistered MDE/power calculation assumed independent per‑arm sampling; the executed shared_initial_candidate semantics (independent_condition_generation=false) remove between‑arm stochasticity and thus make the original MDE inapplicable to the observed contingency.
Bounded repair budget: repairs were bounded to at most one attempt per rejected candidate (maximum_repair_calls_per_task=1); multi‑attempt repair behavior was not tested.
Verifier rule‑set sensitivity: one deterministic verifier/rule set was used; different verifier conservatism will change false‑accept/false‑reject tradeoffs.

Zero discordant pairs: the observed contingency (n10=n01=0) yields degenerate bootstrap CI and McNemar p values; these are arithmetic consequences of the run and must be interpreted conditioned on the executed sampling semantics.
